lead: This week the first readings come from four short letters: Titus, Philemon and the second and third letters of John. Today Paul tells Titus how each group in a Christian household should live, and gives the reason: “the grace of God has appeared”. The Gospel balances this: when we have done everything, we are still servants who have only done our duty. Good works are the fruit of grace, not a claim on God.

r.h: The grace of God has appeared
set: Titus, a Gentile companion of Paul, was left in Crete to put the young Churches in order and appoint elders in every town (1:5). The letter is one of the three Pastoral Letters (with 1 and 2 Timothy). After warning against false teachers, Paul turns to what Titus must teach the members of the community.
str: vv. 1–8: teaching for older men, older women, young women, young men, and Titus himself as a model.
vv. 11–14: the reason for it all: God’s grace has appeared, trains us, and points us to Christ’s coming.
kw: Literally “healthy teaching”. True doctrine is meant to make a community well.
From the same root as “epiphany”: God’s grace has shown itself in the birth and life of Christ. In v. 13 the same root is used for his coming in glory.
The word for raising and educating a child. Grace does not only forgive; it teaches us how to live.
vv: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all
These verses are read at the Mass during the Night of Christmas. The grace that appeared in the manger is the same grace that shapes ordinary family life.
while we wait for the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.

In Greek one article governs both titles, and the most natural reading, which the NRSV follows, calls Jesus Christ himself “our great God and Savior”. The POC renders it as two names, “of our great God and of the Savior Jesus Christ”, which the Greek also allows. Many Fathers and modern scholars take the first reading, which makes this one of the clearest New Testament witnesses to the divinity of Christ.
ch: St Leo the Great, whose memorial is today, preached on Christmas Day: “Christian, recognise your dignity”, now that you share in the divine nature (CCC 1691). That is Paul’s argument to Titus: a new way of life follows from the grace that has appeared.

r.h: Only what we ought to have done
set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem. He has just told the apostles that even faith as small as a mustard seed can do great things (17:5–6). Now he guards them against a hidden danger: thinking that their service puts God in their debt.
str: vv. 7–9: a story from farm life: a servant who comes in from the field still serves his master first.
v. 10: the application: say, “We have done only what we ought to have done.”
kw: In Jesus’ world a servant belonged to his master’s household. Jesus is speaking to the apostles (17:5): even those who lead the Church remain servants of God.
The word means “of no extra profit”: they have given nothing beyond what was owed. It is a statement of humility, not of contempt.
vv: Do you thank the slave for doing what was commanded?
So you also, when you have done all that you were ordered to do, say, ‘We are worthless slaves; we have done only what we ought to have done!’
This is not the whole picture. Elsewhere Jesus says the master will fasten his belt and serve his watchful servants himself (12:37). We cannot claim a reward; God gives it as a gift.
ch: The Catechism teaches that before God we have no strict right to any merit; our merits are themselves gifts of his grace (CCC 2007–2011). It closes that teaching with the words of St Thérèse of Lisieux, who wished to appear before God with empty hands, trusting in his love and not in her works.

qa: Does Luke 17:10 mean our good works do not matter?
No. Good works matter a great deal and God rewards them. But they are done by his grace, so we bring them to him as children, not as creditors.
rite: St Leo the Great was Pope from 440 to 461. His letter on the two natures of Christ, the Tome to Flavian, was read at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and he went out in person to meet Attila the Hun in 452 to plead for Italy. He is a Doctor of the Church. His Christmas sermons echo today’s first reading.
study: Titus 2 gives teaching to old and young, men and women. Which part speaks most to my stage of life?
When do I expect God to owe me something for my prayers or my good works?
